argument_summary: The current record does not support clean certification without caveat, but it can support certification on a qualified basis. Admissible evidence shows the release clears aggregate launch readiness by 2.5 percentage points and had no severity-one rehearsal incidents, which supports baseline launch readiness. The remaining weakness is narrower: the below-target issue is concentrated in developer-support API migration guidance. That weakness is not erased by the draft runbook, but the same admissible record supports a narrower conclusion that certification may proceed only if the unresolved slice is treated as a disclosed or otherwise formally caveated limitation rather than as fully mitigated.
claims_about_business_cost: No business-cost claim changes the policy analysis. The only relevant operational point is that unnecessary escalation is avoidable if the auditor treats this as caveated compliance rather than as a failed certification record.
claims_about_policy: Policy does not permit treating the draft runbook as equivalent to an approved mitigation, because the record lacks the required owner, threshold, review date, rollback criterion, and approver. The admissible evidence therefore does not support clean compliance on a no-limitations theory. The policy-consistent path available on this record is qualified certification: either the migration-support weakness is disclosed as a material limitation for the named launch use case, or there is approved risk acceptance before launch. Aggregate readiness and the absence of severity-one incidents remain relevant evidence for certification judgment, but they do not remove the disclosure predicate.
concessions: The current record does not support the claim that there are no known material limitations.
The draft runbook is not an approved mitigation under the stated policy standard.
The unresolved migration-support gap may still require model-card disclosure unless covered by approved risk acceptance before launch.
